en: The Secret Essential Record Containing Radiance: The Chapter on the Yoga-Siddhi of Vināyaka-gaṇapati.
Because the masters of the past and present have kept this deeply secret, it was not recorded in the sūtras; or,
while the mantras were revealed, their underlying principles were not made manifest.
Scholars of the final age are frequently beset by obstacles;
for this reason, Dharma Master Han-guang personally received this secret meaning of the Dharma from the Venerable Master Amoghavajra as soon as it was transmitted.
I shall now briefly cite and record it for the time being.
The mantra of King Gaṇapati—also known as Vināyaka—is as follows: Oṃ namo vighnāntakāya hūṃ svāhā.
Ṭi-mu-kha-śa-ta-ni-ya-tha-oṃ-na-ya-ka-vi-na-ya-ka-t-ra-ya-ka-pa-li-ka.
*Tra-ya-kṣaṃ-kha-ha-si-ti-kṣaṃ-kha-ka-ci-dhau*.
There are additional phrases that may be appended according to the specific purpose sought, namely:
pacifying (*śāntika*), increasing (*pauṣṭika*), magnetizing (*vaśīkaraṇa*), subjugating (*abhicāruka*), summoning (*ākarṣaṇa*), and so forth.
Its Sanskrit name is Ācārya; it can be differentiated, but in ordinary usage, the term for "pacifying" (*śānti*) is added.
This may be seen in the original ritual manual: *Svāhā*. If one wishes to perform pacification (*śānti*): [insert mantra here].
Add the word *śāntikara* to *svāhā* if one wishes to seek wealth;
add the word *puṣṭikara* to *svāhā*.
If one desires to seek love,
add the phrase "bandha jīrakaraṇa" to the preceding sentence.
If one desires to subdue evil beings...
Omit the preceding phrase and add the phrase for *abhicāruka*.
If one desires to seek the prolongation of life,
omit the preceding phrase and add the phrase for *jānta*.
If one wishes to perform summoning (*ākarṣaṇa*),
add the syllables *Aṅkuśe* to the preceding phrases.
These various words encompass many types of *siddhi*.
The mantra for the two-bodied form of Vināyaka that generates a joyful mind is:
Oṃ Giri-hūṃ. [This includes an additional phrase.
It is to be recited according to the usual procedure as previously described.
"Kṣi-ka-sa-ti-sā-ra-svāhā. If a practitioner constantly recites this mantra, there will be no obstacles.
This is the manifestation of the provisional and ultimate meanings within the mantras. Why is this so?
*Giri* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara.
The Bodhisattva manifests this body as his wife to encourage him and cause the Vināyakas to cease creating obstacles.
There is a past causal connection as explained by other schools;
this constitutes the meaning of the provisional.
Next, the syllable *kṣa* is the seed-syllable of the deity Vināyaka.
This is the ever-attendant Māra.
What is the ever-attendant Māra?
It refers to that which constantly follows all sentient beings, seeking out their vulnerabilities.
However, the celestial māras and terrestrial māras are not like this;
they come only occasionally to create obstacles and difficulties.
The vināyakas, by contrast, constantly follow one about to create obstacles and difficulties.
Therefore, he is called "one who is constantly followed by Māra.
Even if the Brahma Kings, Kauśika, and the various devas, nāgas, and so forth were to attempt it,
they could not overcome such obstacles and difficulties.
Only Avalokiteśvara and the Bodhisattva Kūṭāgāra are able to remove these obstacles caused by the vināyakas.
The Sūtra says: "If one knows that there are various obstacles and difficulties within one's body..."
If the virtuous matters one seeks do not accord with one's wishes,
one should bathe this image of Avalokiteśvara with scented water. Then,
take this water and recite the mantra over it one hundred and eight times.
Bathe the image of the Vināyaka,
then take up the mantra and recite it one hundred and eight times,
sprinkling the water over one's own body as the practitioner.

All obstacles and difficulties will naturally vanish, and whatever one seeks shall be fulfilled according to one's wishes; thus it is said. Use the fundamental mantra of the Eleven-faced Avalokiteśvara.
And one performs the aforementioned rite.
There are many scriptural passages concerning the testimony of the Bodhisattva Kuntali regarding the removal of obstacles caused by Vināyakas.
As extensively explained in other schools, such as the *Dṛṣṭisamuccaya-sūtra* and others, the mantra for subduing the evil of the dual-bodied Vināyakas is:
Oṃ jñaḥ jñaḥ hūṃ svāhā. If a practitioner wishes to bind an evil person, they should employ this mantra.
If one wishes to expel wicked persons, this mantra should also be employed.
This dhāraṇī specifically reveals the meaning of the two realities;
therefore, a single syllable is doubled to form two syllables.
Upon investigating its reality, it is precisely the provisional.
Why is it provisional?
It is because Buddhas and Bodhisattvas employ it in order to subdue all those who are indolent.
This body has manifested.
All obstacles and difficulties arise from indolence;
if one ceases indolence, obstacles and difficulties will not arise.
The provisional immediately accords with the real;
therefore, a single word is repeated.
The real immediately manifests the provisional.
Therefore, know that this is the transformation of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
The Buddha Vairocana then proclaimed:
"It is a body that reaches everywhere."
"I manifest in accordance with the various types of sentient beings in order to transform and deliver them.
Puxian (Samantabhadra) was the very last to appear as a Vināyaka," and so forth. As for the Bodhisattva, it is Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas manifest as male or female deities to transform and deliver sentient beings.
Now, it is said that the forms of Vināyakas are of many kinds;
some resemble humans or devas, while others resemble Brahmins.
Some manifest the handsome forms of men and women,
dividing themselves into four groups to encompass many types;
in such various ways, they create all manner of obstacles.
The Great Holy Deva, King of Joy,
is a body manifested through skillful means,
as described above.
It is because he wishes to entice and advance those who create obstacles so that they may enter into right view;
therefore, he does not manifest with an elephant head like other vināyakas,
as this is intended as a symbolic illustration.
This means that just as an elephant king, despite possessing great strength and anger,
can follow and be nurtured by its keeper and trainer, so too is Gaṇapati.
Although he manifests an obstructed body,
he is able to follow those who take refuge, even up to those who take refuge in the Buddha;
for this reason, this deva manifests his head.
Vināyaka is also called Vinatka;
this is translated as "Elephant Trunk.
His form is like that of a human, but his trunk is exceedingly long.
This is because he is attached to the sensory object of fragrance.
Only this Great Sage Deva has the features of his head,
eyes, ears, nose, and tongue all resembling those of an elephant.
This is because she is able to follow [the practitioner].
This deity is Gaṇapati;
in this language, it means "Joy."
It is not other vināyakas;
by the power of the roots of goodness of loving-kindness and compassion,
it causes all vināyakas to give rise to a heart of joy.
Thereafter, one should reprimand them so that they do not create obstacles.
When they are angry, one may, at will,
bind them with their own nose, whether it be near or far.
Therefore, he is superior to other vināyakas.
Having already explained the provisional and ultimate meanings of the vināyakas,
next the characteristics of the hand-seals (mudrās) will be explained.
Form the outer hand-binding with both hands;
the two index fingers are shaped like jewels.
This is the mudrā-sign; using the aforementioned Great Mantra, again form the inner hand-binding with both hands.
Join the tips of the right middle finger and index finger and hold them upright;
cross the left middle finger and index finger over them,
and join these two fingers together upright as on the right side.
Then, place the index fingers of both hands alongside the backs of the middle fingers, with the thumbs standing side by side.
This mudrā uses the second mantra mentioned previously; it is further based on the previous mudrā.
Change the left and right little fingers and ring fingers to form the outer binding.
This mudrā is used with the third mantra mentioned previously. Next, the Semblance Dharma is described:
it has the head of an elephant and the body of a human.
The left tooth protrudes and the right tooth is broken;
the face is slightly turned to the left,
and the nose is slanted outward.
The body is reddish-yellow in color and has six arms.

The upper left hand holds a sword (according to Vajrajñāna, it holds a blade); the next hand holds a fruit plate (according to Vajrajñāna, it holds a *modaka* sweetmeat); and the lower hand holds a wheel.
The upper right hand holds a handle;
the next hand holds a rope;
the lower hand holds a tusk.
If one recites the aforementioned Great Mantra before this image, all that is sought shall be accomplished.
Furthermore, there are two deities with celestial bodies embracing each other, standing upright upon a pair of elephant heads with human torsos.
The deity on its left wears a celestial flower crown;
its nose and tusks are short, and its eyes are likewise narrow. It wears a red *kāṣāya*, the robe of the field of merit.
The body is the color of white flesh;
the face of the deity on the right is not benevolent,
with a long nose and wide eyes.
He does not wear a celestial crown or the robes of a field of merit;
his body is reddish-yellow in color,
and he merely wraps a black garment around his neck and shoulders.
This deva brings his face close to the face of the female deva before him,
manifesting an expression of affection;
this image reveals the aspect of the provisional and the ultimate.
Before this image, recite the second mantra as before to increase virtue and eliminate evil. Furthermore, the two forms are as previously described, standing upright in embrace;
however, the face of the male deity is positioned over the right shoulder of the female deity.
Furthermore, they gaze at the back of the female deity;
likewise, they fasten the face of the female deity to the right shoulder of the male deity and gaze at his back.
Those with narrow eyes and short teeth are the husbands of these goddesses.
Both of these goddesses do not wear dharma robes or celestial crowns,
but manifest in their original forms as Vināyakas.
Before this image, recite the third mantra first;
all evil matters will be completely extinguished.
This is the method for painting the image according to the essential meaning of the mantras and mudrās of King Gaṇapati.
Having thus spoken, when one is about to practice this dharma,
one should first pay homage to Mahāvairocana,
and next pay homage to Avalokiteśvara.
If one subsequently pays homage to Krodha-vaśī (Muṇḍarī), one will immediately obtain efficacious results.
Samantaprabha and Avalokiteśvara are his primary deities;
Krodha-vaśī is his subduer.
This is why one first offers salutation and respect.
The One of Great and Vast Wisdom said:
"If there are obstacles or hindrances caused by vināyakas,"
One should practice the methods of mantra.
Within these methods of mantra there are three families;
these three families are the three honored ones.
The Three Honored Ones are the Buddha, the Bodhisattva, and the Vajra;
the Buddha, the Bodhisattva, and the Vajra are Vairocana, Avalokiteśvara, and Krodha-vajrapāṇi (Muṇḍalī).
These are the teachings of the three families.
It is able to restrain the indolence of the three karmas;
because it eliminates that indolence,
obstacles and difficulties are forever severed and do not arise.
Therefore, those who wish to practice the *jñānapaṭḥi* (wisdom) dharma should first pay homage to Vairocana, Avalokiteśvara, and Krodharāja;
these are the honored ones of the three families.
Because he is able to eliminate the indolence of the practitioner’s body, speech,
and mind, he manifests this form of a Vināyaka;
he is not any other obstructing spirit.
He is known solely by the name Gaṇapati.
The five-syllable mantra of Vairocana is: Oṃ Vīra Hūṃ Phaṭ.
Regarding the eleven-faced Avalokiteśvara and the various mantras and Sanskrit names spoken by all the Buddhas, they may be found in the scriptures translated by Amoghavajra.

Oṃ nara nara diri diri duru duru iṭi viṭi ceṭi ceṭi pra-ceṭi pra-ceṭi ku-sume ku-soma-vale iri miri cirī cirī ciri-jvara-praśamana-pramathana-sarva-sattva-mahā-kāruṇika svāhā. The mantra of the Bodhisattva Kuṇḍalī for removing obstacles and difficulties is as follows: Oṃ nara nara diri diri duru duru iṭi viṭi ceṭi ceṭi pra-ceṭi pra-ceṭi ku-sume ku-soma-vale iri miri cirī cirī ciri-jvara-praśamana-pramathana-sarva-sattva-mahā-kāruṇika svāhā.

Namo ratnatrayāya | Namo vajrapāṇaye mahāyakṣasenāpataye | Namo vajrakrodhāya | Oṃ hulu hulu ṭiṣṭha ṭiṣṭha bandha bandha dhāraya dhāraya amṛte hūṃ phaṭ | Such is the subtle and profound secret meaning as above.
In the final age, the wise should keep this secret.
It should be placed among the Sanskrit scriptures (brahman-puṭa).
Do not recklessly transmit it to those who are not fit vessels.
What is meant by "not being a vessel"?
It refers to those who lack wisdom and lack faith,
as well as wicked people, those who do not guard their speech, and so forth.
These are not individuals who are fit vessels for the Dharma.
If one were to freely proclaim [these teachings] before such people,
I fear they would incur the sin of slander.
Therefore, those who do not select their ritual vessels will encounter obstacles and difficulties;
for this reason, I have now further established these regulations.
A wise person who practices them will swiftly attain *siddhi*.
